headline: Candles, Dying Families, and the Quant Firm That Prints Money
lede: A satirical 1,400-word story of a Jane Street interview—complete with a $3,600 candle budget and a family listed as "dying"—went briefly viral, which is either a sign that finance Twitter has lost the plot or, more charitably, that it has finally developed a sense of humor about the absurdist logic at the heart of modern prop trading.
body:
The interview, as recounted in the satirical post, takes place in 2013: a candidate is handed a spreadsheet budget to "optimize," featuring line items that include "candles: $3,600" and, where one might expect a dependant allowance, simply "family: dying." After a long silence in which the candidate presumably weighs the net present value of grief, the correct answer is revealed—dump $3,750 worth of candles into the market at precisely 10:00:01 every morning to "provide liquidity to candle ETFs during the U.S. cash open." The absurdism is pitch-perfect, not despite but because of its internal logic: in a firm that made its fortune threading the eye of ETF creation-redemption arbitrage, there really is no asset class too humble to become a liquidity event.

Jane Street did not spring fully formed from some hedge-fund fever dream. Founded in 1999 by a handful of defectors from Susquehanna International Group, it spent its early years as an unremarkable equity-options shop before discovering, sometime around the mid-2000s, that exchange-traded funds were an arbitrage machine hiding in plain sight. Today the firm controls roughly 41% of U.S. bond ETF trading volume, 24% of all listed ETF activity, and generates north of $39 billion in annual net trading revenue with a workforce of approximately 3,500—yielding something in the neighborhood of $11 million per employee. That number, which appears in the OCR table circulating alongside the satire, is not a typo.

The table placing Jane Street seventh on a profit-per-employee ranking is itself a minor masterpiece of compressed information. Above it sit firms that most civilians have never heard of: XTX Markets, a London-based algorithmic market maker with around 300 people generating over $33 million in revenue per head; Hudson River Trading, an even more opaque New York outfit of roughly 350 that posted $12.3 billion in full-year 2025 revenue—$8 to $10 million per employee by most estimates. At the summit sits Valve Corporation, the games company that owns Steam, which earns an estimated $48 million per employee and employs around 350 people to run what is effectively a global software distribution monopoly. That Valve shares the top of a prop-trading leaderboard is its own quiet joke: the firm publishes no financial statements, makes no earnings calls, and describes its management philosophy as self-directed project selection. Its business model, if anything, makes Jane Street's look labor-intensive.

What the satire captures with particular fidelity is the peculiar epistemology of the Jane Street interview. Unlike investment-banking processes, which test candidates' knowledge of valuation multiples and precedent transactions, Jane Street's intake is pointedly incurious about finance. Interviewers do not ask about the Fed or recent deals. What they do is hand you a game—sometimes dice, sometimes cards, often a fictional commodity—and watch how you build a market. Pen and paper are permitted; computers and calculators are not. The firm published its own prep guide, "Probability and Markets," which telegraphs the aesthetic: expected value, Bayesian updating, and the behavior of prices under uncertainty. The candle ETF punchline works because it correctly identifies the form of reasoning the firm prizes: not what do candles cost, but what is the optimal execution strategy for a candle position at the open.

The viral moment arrived at a time when Jane Street's public profile has become, by the firm's historical standards, almost garish. Its 2025 compensation pool of $9.4 billion—on top of entry-level packages already running $250,000 to $300,000—has made it the subject of breathless coverage that the firm itself declines to comment on. The internet's response has been to generate an entire genre of fictional interview encounters: a candidate asked to market-make a chess game in Washington Square Park, an interviewer on the StairMaster at Equinox asking about implied volatility on his rice allocation, each vignette ending identically—no offer extended. The candle story fits the template but adds something the others lack: a genuine structural joke about what ETF market-making actually involves, which is the industrialization of arbitrage so complete that the underlying instrument becomes irrelevant. Candles, bond ETFs, rice at Panda Express—the spread is the spread.

That the same table includes NVIDIA twice—once for the parent company at roughly $14.9 million profit per employee among its 46,000 staff, and again in what appears to be a data quirk at a different headcount—and lists Anthropic and OpenAI with asterisks suggesting the numbers are projections rather than audited results, only adds to the document's charm as a piece of financial folk art. The real firms are extraordinary enough. HRT, which describes itself as employing "quants, scientists, and engineers," spent $1 billion on AI infrastructure in 2025 and posts returns that would make a macro fund manager quietly weep. Citadel Securities, with 1,100 employees and $6.6 million in estimated profit per head, barely registers in the popular imagination despite running one of the largest equity market-making operations on earth. The table exists to make the point that the most structurally profitable businesses of the early twenty-first century are not the ones selling things to consumers but the ones that have quietly made themselves indispensable to the plumbing of capital markets—or, in Valve's case, to the plumbing of digital leisure.

concepts.definition: Proprietary trading, in which a firm deploys its own capital rather than clients' money to generate returns. Prop firms like Jane Street, HRT, and XTX Markets keep all gains internally and bear all losses, which concentrates both the upside and the incentive to hire very selectively.

The practice of continuously quoting both a bid and an offer price for a security, earning the spread between them in exchange for providing liquidity. Jane Street's dominance in ETF market making means it stands as the buyer and seller of last resort for a substantial share of daily U.S. equity-fund trading volume.

A metric dividing a firm's net income (or, where unavailable, net trading revenue) by its headcount, used to compare capital efficiency across businesses with very different labor models. It tends to flatter firms that operate leveraged financial businesses or platform monopolies—where marginal revenue is nearly all profit—rather than manufacturers or retailers that require proportional headcount growth.

fact_check: The Jane Street interview described in the post is satirical fiction — no such 2013 encounter occurred, and the candle-ETF scenario is an invented absurdist punchline. The prop-trading firms named in the accompanying table (Jane Street, XTX Markets, HRT, Citadel Securities, NVIDIA, Hyperliquid, Tether, Anthropic, OpenAI, Craigslist, Valve) are all real; the revenue and profit-per-employee figures are approximate estimates drawn from public filings, press reports, and analyst calculations as of 2024–2025, not audited accounts. Valve, Jane Street, XTX, HRT, and Craigslist are private and do not publish financials; figures for those firms should be treated as well-sourced estimates rather than verified data. Anthropic and OpenAI figures are marked with asterisks in the original table, suggesting they are projections.
